Jeremiah — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Jeremiah was a priest from Anathoth, a town in the territory of Benjamin.

God called him to be a prophet when he was very young, about seventy years after Isaiah's death according to Henry's chronology.

Jeremiah continued serving faithfully for about forty years, until Judah's sins reached their full measure and national destruction followed.

The prophecies preserved in this book are not arranged in the order in which Jeremiah delivered them.

Henry notes that Benjamin Blayney attempted to arrange them more regularly, in this order:

Jeremiah 1–20; 22; 23; 25; 26; 35; 36; 45; 24; 29; 30; 31; 27; 28; 21; 34; 37; 32; 33; 38; 39:15–18, followed by 39:1–14; 40–44; 46–52.

This is a report of Blayney's proposed reading sequence, not a recommendation to rearrange the canonical biblical text or its SWORD versification.

Jeremiah's prophecies chiefly concern the idolatry and other sins of Judah, the threatened judgments, the future restoration and deliverance, and promises concerning the Messiah.

They are especially marked by plain and faithful rebukes, affectionate appeals and grave warnings.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJeremiah's call to the prophetic office.1–10A vision of an almond-tree and of a seething-pot, Divine protection is promised.11–19
Jeremiah is called to speak God's word (verses 1–10)

Jeremiah received his call to prophetic service when he was still young.

He was appointed to speak not only to the Jews, but also to the neighboring nations.

Through the book he remains a prophet whose warnings concern the whole world.

It would be well for everyone to take those warnings seriously.

The Lord who formed us knows the particular duties and purposes for which he intends us.

But unless he makes us holy through his Spirit who creates new life, we will not be fit for his holy service on earth or his holy happiness in heaven.

We should think humbly of ourselves.

Young people should remember their inexperience and not presume to undertake tasks beyond their abilities.

Yet an awareness of our weakness and inadequacy should make us approach our work with humility, not cause us to draw back when God calls.

Those commissioned to deliver messages from God must not fear human opposition.

Through a sign, the Lord gave Jeremiah the gift needed for the task.

God's message must be delivered in God's own words.

Whatever worldly advisers or politicians believe, the true security of a kingdom is ultimately determined by God's purpose and word.

The almond tree, boiling pot and promised protection (verses 11–19)

God showed Jeremiah the approaching destruction of Judah and Jerusalem by the Chaldeans.

The almond tree, which blossoms earlier in spring than other trees, indicated how soon the judgment would come.

God also showed where the approaching destruction would originate.

Jeremiah saw a boiling pot, a picture of Judah and Jerusalem thrown into terrible turmoil.

The pot's opening, or the face of the furnace beneath it, pointed toward the north.

From that direction would come the fire and the fuel that would consume Judah.

Northern powers would unite.

The cause of these judgments was Judah's sin.

Jeremiah was to declare the whole counsel of God, not merely the parts that pleased his listeners.

Reverence for God is the best remedy for fear of people.

It is better to have every human being against us than to have God as our enemy.

Those who know that God is with them do not need to fear anyone who opposes them.

Let us pray for the willingness to give up our private interests whenever necessary, and for steadfastness so that nothing draws us away from duty.
classic_reading:
[Jer.1.1-Jer.1.10]
Jeremiah
Jeremiah was a priest, a native of Anathoth, in the tribe of Benjamin. He was called to the prophetic office when very young, about seventy years after the death of Isaiah, and exercised it for about forty years with great faithfulness, till the sins of the Jewish nation came to their full measure and destruction followed. The prophecies of Jeremiah do not stand as they were delivered. Blayney has endeavoured to arrange them in more regular order, namely, Jr 1-20; 22; 23; 25; 26; 35; 36; 45; 24; 29; 30; 31; 27; 28; 21; 34; 37; 32; 33; 38; 39:15-18, 1-14; 40-44; 46-52. The general subject of his prophecies is the idolatry and other sins of the Jews; the judgments by which they were threatened, with references to their future restoration and deliverance, and promises of the Messiah. They are remarkable for plain and faithful reproofs, affectionate expostulations, and awful warnings.
Chapter 1
Jeremiah's call to the prophetic office. ( [Jer.1.1-Jer.1.10] Jr 1:1-10) A vision of an almond-tree and of a seething-pot, Divine protection is promised. ( [Jer.1.11-Jer.1.19] Jr 1:11-19)
Verses 1-10 Jeremiah's early call to the work and office of a prophet is stated. He was to be a prophet, not to the Jews only, but to the neighbouring nations. He is still a prophet to the whole world, and it would be well if they would attend to these warnings. The Lord who formed us, knows for what particular services and purposes he intended us. But unless he sanctify us by his new-creating Spirit, we shall neither be fit for his holy service on earth, nor his holy happiness in heaven. It becomes us to have low thoughts of ourselves. Those who are young, should consider that they are so, and not venture beyond their powers. But though a sense of our own weakness and insufficiency should make us go humbly about our work, it should not make us draw back when God calls us. Those who have messages to deliver from God, must not fear the face of man. The Lord, by a sign, gave Jeremiah such a gift as was necessary. God's message should be delivered in his own words. Whatever wordly wise men or politicians may think, the safety of kingdoms is decided according to the purpose and word of God.
[Jer.1.11-Jer.1.19]
Verses 11-19 God gave Jeremiah a view of the destruction of Judah and Jerusalem by the Chaldeans. The almond-tree, which is more forward in the spring than any other, represented the speedy approach of judgments. God also showed whence the intended ruin should arise. Jeremiah saw a seething-pot boiling, representing Jerusalem and Judah in great commotion. The mouth or face of the furnace or hearth, was toward the north; from whence the fire and fuel were to come. The northern powers shall unite. The cause of these judgments was the sin of Judah. The whole counsel of God must be declared. The fear of God is the best remedy against the fear of man. Better to have all men our enemies than God our enemy; those who are sure they have God with them, need not, ought not to fear, whoever is against them. Let us pray that we may be willing to give up personal interests, and that nothing may move us from our duty.

God reminds his people of their early devotion (verses 1–8)

People who begin well and then fail to persevere will rightly be reminded of how promising their beginnings once were.

Those who abandon a faith they once professed often oppose it more fiercely than people who never knew it.

Such people have no adequate excuse for their departure.

God's spiritual Israel should acknowledge the debt owed to him for bringing them safely through the wilderness of this world, where so many dangers threaten the soul.

How sad that people who once appeared devoted to the Lord later live in ways that make their earlier religious profession an added witness against their sins!

As we grow in knowledge, let us be careful not to lose zeal and warmth of devotion.

The fountain of life is exchanged for broken cisterns (verses 9–13)

Before the Lord punishes sinners, he pleads with them, calling them to repentance.

The charges he brings are the very matters we should confront within ourselves.

We should tremble at the anger and curse toward which people run when they reject God's favor and grace.

Grace in Jesus Christ is like water from a spring.

It refreshes, cools, cleanses and brings fruit.

It is living water because it gives life to dead sinners, revives believers who are growing weary, sustains spiritual life, and leads to eternal life.

It flows without being exhausted.

Abandoning this Fountain is the first great evil.

God's professing people do so when they neglect his word and appointed worship.

Instead they dig broken cisterns that cannot hold water.

These are the world and its possessions, along with human inventions that people trust and follow.

Let us cling wholeheartedly to the Lord alone.

Where else could we go?

How readily we surrender the consolations of the Holy Spirit for the worthless excitements enjoyed by enthusiastic but hypocritical people!

Israel suffers the consequences of rebellion (verses 14–19)

Was Israel intended to live as a slave?

No. They were the descendants of Abraham.

Henry makes a spiritual application.

Was the human soul created to be enslaved?

No. Yet through sin it has sold its freedom and made itself captive to many sinful desires and passions.

Assyrian rulers, like lions, overpowered Israel.

People from Egypt also destroyed the nation's strength and splendor.

Israel brought those calamities upon itself by turning away from God.

The practical warning is simple:

Repent of sin, so that correction does not become destruction.

What business does a Christian have pursuing forbidden pleasures, empty sinful amusements, greed or ambition?

Judah's fruitless pursuit of sin (verses 20–28)

Despite all the advantages Judah had received, the people became like a wild vine producing poisonous fruit.

People can become as enslaved to uncontrolled desires and lusts as irrational animals are to their instincts.

God warned them not to exhaust themselves pursuing things that could bring only distress and misery.

We should never despair of the extent of God's mercy, which is sufficient to pardon our sins.

Nor should we despair of the power of his grace, which can overcome even the strongest corruption in our hearts.

Empty confidence and continued self-justification (verses 29–37)

God's judgments had failed to change the people.

Instead, they tried to justify themselves.

For people who make the world their true home and final portion, it becomes a wilderness and a dark country.

But those who dwell in God can say their inheritance has fallen in pleasant places.

The people's words reveal the presumption of sinners who have long stopped thinking seriously about the Lord.

How many days pass in our own lives without remembering him as we should!

The Lord was displeased with Judah's false confidences and would not make them succeed.

People may use all their cleverness, but they cannot find happiness through sin or discover any honest excuse for it.

They may move from one sin to another.

But no one ever hardened the heart against God, turned away from him and truly prospered.

Verses 1-8 Those who begin well, but do not persevere, will justly be upbraided with their hopeful and promising beginnings. Those who desert religion, commonly oppose it more than those who never knew it. For this they could have no excuse. God's spiritual Israel must own their obligations to him for safe conduct through the wilderness of this world, so dangerous to the soul. Alas, that many, who once appeared devoted to the Lord, so live that their professions aggravate their crimes! Let us be careful that we do not lose in zeal and fervency, as we gain knowledge.
[Jer.2.9-Jer.2.13]
Verses 9-13 Before God punishes sinners, he pleads with them, to bring them to repentance. He pleads with us, what we should plead with ourselves. Be afraid to think of the wrath and curse which will be the portion of those who throw themselves out of God's grace and favour. Grace in Christ is compared to water from a fountain, it being cooling and refreshing, cleansing and making fruitful: to living water, because it quickens dead sinners, revives drooping saints, supports and maintains spiritual life, and issues in eternal life, and is ever-flowing. To forsake this Fountain is the first evil; this is done when the people of God neglect his word and ordinances. They hewed them out broken cisterns, that could hold no water. Such are the world, and the things in it; such are the inventions of men when followed and depended on. Let us, with purpose of heart, cleave to the Lord only; whither else shall we go? How prone are we to forego the consolations of the Holy Spirit, for the worthless joys of the enthusiast and hypocrite!
[Jer.2.14-Jer.2.19]
Verses 14-19 Is Israel a servant? No, they are the seed of Abraham. We may apply this spiritually: Is the soul of man a slave? No, it is not; but has sold its own liberty, and enslaved itself to divers lusts and passions. The Assyrian princes, like lions, prevailed against Israel. People from Egypt destroyed their glory and strength. They brought these calamities on themselves by departing from the Lord. The use and application of this is, Repent of thy sin, that thy correction may not be thy ruin. What has a Christian to do in the ways of forbidden pleasure or vain sinful mirth, or with the pursuits of covetousness and ambition?
[Jer.2.20-Jer.2.28]
Verses 20-28 Notwithstanding all their advantages, Israel had become like the wild vine that bears poisonous fruit. Men are often as much under the power of their unbridled desires and their sinful lusts, as the brute beasts. But the Lord here warns them not to weary themselves in pursuits which could only bring distress and misery. As we must not despair of the mercy of God, but believe that to be sufficient for the pardon of our sins, so neither must we despair of the grace of God, but believe that it is able to subdue our corruptions, though ever so strong.
[Jer.2.29-Jer.2.37]
Verses 29-37 The nation had not been wrought upon by the judgements of God, but sought to justify themselves. The world is, to those who make it their home and their portion, a wilderness and a land of darkness; but those who dwell in God, have the lines fallen to them in pleasant places. Here is the language of presumptuous sinners. The Jews had long thrown off serious thoughts of God. How many days of our lives pass without suitable remembrance of him! The Lord was displeased with their confidences, and would not prosper them therein. Men employ all their ingenuity, but cannot find happiness in the way of sin, or excuse for it. They may shift from one sin to another, but none ever hardened himself against God, or turned from him, and prospered.

God invites the unfaithful to return (verses 1–5)

When we repent, it is good to remember the particular sins we have committed, including the places where we committed them and the people whose company encouraged them.

How gently the Lord had corrected his people!

When he receives repentant sinners, he acts as God, not merely as a human being.

Whatever you have said or done in the past, will you not turn to him from this moment forward?

Will not such grace overcome your stubbornness?

Now that pardon is announced, will you not accept its benefit?

Repentant people may expect the tender compassion of a Father welcoming a returning prodigal.

They approach him as the Guide of their youth.

Young people especially need guidance.

Those returning to God can take courage from the promise that he will not remain angry forever.

All his mercies throughout history encourage us in the same way.

What could be more desirable for a young person than to have the Lord as Father and Guide?

Parents should earnestly direct their children, day after day, to seek that blessing.

Judah's guilt is greater than Israel's (verses 6–11)

When we consider the sins committed by people who have abandoned a profession of faith, and the consequences that followed, we find abundant reason to avoid their paths.

It is dreadful to be shown more guilty than those who have already perished through their wrongdoing.

But knowing that others were even more wicked will be little comfort in everlasting judgment.

Pardon and restoration are promised (verses 12–20)

Notice how willing God is to forgive sin, and the blessings he has prepared for the age of the gospel.

These promises were proclaimed toward the north, addressing Israel's ten tribes who were captive in Assyria.

They are told how to return to God.

If we confess our sins, the Lord is faithful and just to forgive.

Henry also sees these promises reaching toward a future return of the Jews in later ages.

God graciously receives those who come back to him and, by his grace, calls them out from among others.

The ark of the covenant was not recovered after the exile.

The earlier dispensation was destined to pass away.

Henry connects this transition with the great increase of believers as Gentiles and Israelites scattered among them were brought into God's church.

The prophecy describes a happy condition for God's people.

The Lord can teach people everywhere to call him Father.

Yet no one can truly be his child without a thorough change of heart and life.

Without that renewal, we have no security against wandering away again.

Repentance acknowledges that only God can save (verses 21–25)

Sin means turning aside into crooked paths.

At the root of every sin lies forgetfulness of the Lord our God.

By sin we bring trouble upon ourselves.

But God promises to heal the backsliding of those who return.

That healing comes through his pardoning mercy, his peace that quiets the heart and his grace that renews us.

Repentant people devote themselves to God.

They reject every hope of rescue that depends on anyone else.

They trust in the Lord alone, because only he can save.

These promises point to the great salvation from sin accomplished by Jesus Christ.

Those who repent acknowledge God's justice in their troubles and condemn their own wrongdoing.

They learn to call sin shameful, even the sins in which they once found the greatest pleasure.

They come to recognize sin as death and ruin, and understand that it is responsible for their misery.

People who harden themselves in sin will receive contempt and distress.

Those who conceal their sins will not prosper.

But those who confess and forsake them find mercy.

Return to God sincerely (verses 1–2)

The first two verses of this chapter should be read together with the end of chapter 3.

Sin must be removed from the heart.

Otherwise, it has not been removed from God's sight, because the entire heart is open before him.

The hard heart must be broken up (verses 3–4)

A heart that has never been humbled resembles ground left untilled.

It is ground capable of improvement and entrusted to us for cultivation.

But it lies unused and is covered in thorns and weeds, the natural growth of a corrupt heart.

Let us beg God to create a clean heart in us and to renew a right spirit within us.

Unless a person is born again, that person cannot enter heaven's kingdom.

Judah is warned of an approaching invader (verses 5–18)

A fierce conqueror who had already defeated the surrounding nations would bring desolation upon Judah.

Jeremiah was distressed that false prophets had soothed the people into a dangerous feeling of security.

He described the enemy's approach.

Some attention had been paid in Jerusalem to outward reform.

But this was not enough.

The people's hearts needed washing, through true repentance and faith, to remove the love and pollution of sin.

When lesser troubles do not awaken sinners or bring nations to reform, a more decisive judgment will be pronounced.

The Lord's voice announces that misery is approaching.

Henry especially warns those who profess the gospel but live wickedly.

When judgment falls, the bitterness of sin's fruit and the fatal nature of its end will become undeniable.

Jeremiah grieves over Judah's coming ruin (verses 19–31)

The prophet took no pleasure in announcing messages of divine anger.

In a vision he saw the whole land thrown into confusion.

Compared with its former condition, everything had fallen into disorder.

Yet Judah's ruin would not be final.

The end of a particular earthly comfort is not necessarily the end of everything.

The Lord may correct his people with great severity, but he will not abandon them entirely.

Cosmetics, ornaments and flattering appearances will offer no protection from the coming disaster.

Neither outward privileges, religious profession nor human schemes can prevent judgment.

How miserable are people who remain like foolish children in matters concerning their souls!

Whatever else we fail to understand, may God give us wisdom in the ways of godliness.

Sin will ultimately find the sinner.

And sorrow, sooner or later, will find those who feel secure while rejecting God's warnings.

A profession of religion without integrity (verses 1–9)

Jerusalem could offer no one who behaved with the integrity and godliness God required. The Lord saw the people's true character through every disguise.

The poor were ignorant of God and his ways, and this ignorance led them into wickedness. Those who know nothing of God and true religion may be expected to produce the works of darkness.

But poverty itself does not make people ignorant or wicked. God has faithful people among the poor who know his way, walk in it, and do their duty.

The people Jeremiah condemned were willfully ignorant. They had chosen not to learn; their ignorance could not excuse their conduct.

The rich, meanwhile, were proud and insolent. By abusing the favors God had given them, they made their guilt worse.

God places a limit upon approaching destruction (verses 10–18)

Multitudes are ruined because they believe that God will not judge as strictly as his word declares. Satan used that same deception to bring ruin upon humanity.

Sinners are unwilling to accept any teaching as God's word if it requires them to abandon sin or disturbs their pleasure in it.

By mocking and mistreating the Lord's messengers, Judah filled up the measure of its wickedness.

God can bring suffering upon us from distant places and unexpected causes.

Yet he still had mercy reserved for his people. Therefore he placed limits on this approaching devastation.

Do not overlook God's word “nevertheless” in verse 18.

Here the Lord remembers his covenant with Israel: he displays his holiness and complete opposition to sin while still sparing the sinner (Psalm 89:30–35).

Sin explains the nation's suffering (verses 19–31)

Hearts that have never been humbled readily accuse God of treating them unjustly when suffering arrives.

But sinners may read the nature of their sin in their punishment. If we ask why the Lord permits such distress, we should examine our own wrongdoing.

The restless waves obey the boundary God has set for them. Even a sandy shore restrains the sea as effectively as a mountain, because the Lord has commanded it.

Yet human beings break through every restraint of his law and surrender themselves to wickedness.

They also disregard their own true interests.

Year after year the Lord gives the appointed weeks of harvest. People continually receive his generosity, yet rebel against the Giver.

Sin deprives us of blessings. It can make the heavens like bronze and the earth like iron.

The things of this world cannot be the best things. We must not conclude that God approves of wicked conduct simply because a wicked person enjoys prosperity.

The sentence against evil may be delayed, but it will certainly be carried out.

The question “Shall I not punish them for these things?” announces both the certainty and necessity of God's righteous judgments.

Those who follow sinful paths should remember that those paths have an end—and their final outcome will be bitter.

Judah ignores reason, conscience, Providence and Scripture (verses 4–13)

What brought this disaster upon the people?

Henry identifies four causes.

First, they refused to listen to reason. They would not exercise ordinary prudence concerning the eternal welfare of their own souls. Sin is a falling back—from the road to life toward the road to destruction.

Second, they refused to listen to conscience. They would not take the first step of genuine repentance: asking seriously what wrong they had done, convinced that they had acted wrongly.

Third, they failed to consider God's Providence and recognize his voice within it (Jeremiah 8:7). They did not use the seasons of grace he gave them. Many boast of religious knowledge, yet without the teaching of God's Spirit, even the natural instinct of birds and other creatures guides them more reliably than their supposed wisdom.

Fourth, they refused to attend to the written word of God. Many people possess ample opportunities to learn: Bibles, ministers and other means of grace. Yet they have all these resources without truly benefiting from them.

They would soon be ashamed of their own schemes.

The people posing as especially wise were the priests and false prophets.

Those leaders flattered others in their sins until the flattery led toward destruction.

They quieted fear and silenced complaints with the assurance, “Everything is well.”

Self-interested teachers promise peace when there is no peace.

Thus sinners encourage one another to continue in wrongdoing.

But when the day of judgment comes, they will find nowhere to hide.
